stories.headline: Abu Dhabi Talks End With a Large Prisoner Exchange Agreed but No Ceasefire
stories.what_happened: Two days of US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi ended on Wednesday 11 November with an agreement in principle on a large exchange of prisoners of war. There was no breakthrough on a ceasefire or on territory. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are due to meet Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday and then Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Dublin.
stories.why_it_matters: The exchange would bring many captured soldiers home, but the questions that decide whether the war ends, territory and security, remain unsettled, and Europe is still outside the main room.

key_facts.fact: Two days of US-mediated Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, ended on Wednesday 11 November 2026 with an agreement in principle on a major prisoner exchange.
The exchange was the only tangible result; there was no breakthrough on a ceasefire or on territorial disputes.
US envoy Jared Kushner announced the deal on Wednesday and said the final prisoner numbers would be set on Thursday.
Kushner called it 'the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners' and 'one of the positives'.
Ukraine's chief negotiator Rustem Umerov and Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky both confirmed the exchange; neither gave details on timing or scale.
On Tuesday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said negotiators had discussed exchanging 1,000 prisoners from each side, possibly rising to 1,500 each.
These were the first direct Kyiv-Moscow negotiations in nine months; an earlier round in Geneva in February 2026 produced no breakthrough.
In May 2025, talks in Istanbul also produced an agreement to exchange 1,000 prisoners each, without a ceasefire.
Kushner said of a Putin-Zelenskyy meeting that more work is needed: 'we are pushing a boulder uphill'. He said 'there is not great trust or love between the leaders'.
Kushner said the US speaks daily with both Zelenskyy's team and Putin's team.
Kushner and Steve Witkoff were to travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet Putin, then go to Dublin for talks with Zelenskyy.

Ukrainian negotiator Davyd Arakhamia described the talks as among the most difficult, said Russian representatives had strict instructions, and called for another round 'as soon as possible', hoping for a solution before the new year.
Zelenskyy, on a state visit to Copenhagen, was briefed by video call; he said 'ending this war and providing security guarantees' must come first.
Russia demands that Ukraine withdraw from the part of the Donbas region still under Kyiv's control; Zelenskyy says territorial decisions must be made at the leaders' level.
Moscow rejects an immediate ceasefire and wants broader security arrangements first.
European representatives were in Abu Dhabi for separate consultations with Ukrainian and US officials; they did not take part in the trilateral talks.
Medinsky said Russia had not held talks with Europeans: 'We don't really understand in what capacity they are here.' He said Moscow had received no concrete European peace proposals.
Washington indicated that European countries should eventually join the negotiations, particularly on future security arrangements.
The talks focused mainly on humanitarian issues: prisoner exchanges, returning Ukrainian civilians held in captivity, and children taken from Ukraine. Security guarantees were also discussed.
Medinsky said mutual understanding was reached on some issues and more talks will be held.
Zelenskyy, who was in Copenhagen and did not attend, called the second day 'constructive and quite substantive'.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the meeting 'very productive' but said a breakthrough to end the war will take time.
Representatives from European governments, the EU and NATO were in Abu Dhabi and consulted with Ukraine's delegation. Zelenskyy said European security cannot be considered 'without Europe'.
Ukraine is reeling from aerial attacks on its power grid; little territory has changed hands on the front line this year; the war has lasted nearly five years.

Overnight, Russia struck Zaporizhzhia and Kharkiv, wounding seven civilians. Russia's Defence Ministry said it downed 627 Ukrainian drones overnight; drones started a fire at the Ust-Luga port, a major oil export facility.
The final session on Wednesday ran just under two hours. Medinsky, an adviser to President Putin, said details of the exchange would be announced 'shortly'.
Medinsky said security arrangements for Ukraine and Europe were a central focus: 'In some places we reached an understanding, in other places we did not.'

Medinsky repeated Moscow's claim to parts of Ukraine: 'every inch of our land will be returned to Russia. One way or another.' Ukraine rejects giving up any territory it currently controls as a condition for peace.
Russia's broader demands include territorial concessions, demilitarisation and major political changes in Kyiv.

US officials told the Financial Times they want to resolve the war and continental security arrangements together and that European officials should have a seat at the table; Moscow has so far rejected a European role.
Zelenskyy landed in Ireland on Wednesday 11 November and met Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheal Martin at Government Buildings in Dublin.
In Dublin, Zelenskyy said between 1,000 and 1,200 prisoners of war may be exchanged.
The European Political Community (EPC) summit is in Dublin on Thursday 12 November at the Convention Centre Dublin; Zelenskyy is due to speak. Ireland holds the EU Council presidency for six months.
Kushner said the Dublin meeting would be a 'debrief' and that the US sees 'some openings and some opportunities'.
On the Donbas region, Zelenskyy said Ukraine could not discuss abandoning it. The Taoiseach said Ukrainians deserve a 'just and lasting peace' and that Ukraine's future 'is in the European Union'.

Moscow also wants a ban on Ukrainian NATO membership and limits on Ukraine's military. Ukraine proposes an unconditional ceasefire as the first step toward broader talks; the Kremlin has repeatedly dismissed this.
Donbas is a partially occupied, strategically important region in eastern Ukraine. Zelensky will attend an informal meeting of EU leaders on 13 November.

stories.headline: World Leaders Address COP31 as Turkey Pushes a Pledge to Electrify More of the World's Energy
stories.what_happened: About 40 leaders addressed the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Wednesday 11 November. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, at his final COP, said fossil fuels 'must go the way of the dinosaurs'. Host Turkey is promoting a voluntary '35 by 35' pledge to raise electricity's share of energy use from 23% to 35% by 2035; thirteen countries have publicly backed it, while many big names stayed away from the summit.
stories.why_it_matters: Switching cars, heating and factories to electricity can cut the use of oil, gas and coal, but only if the electricity is clean; that argument, and who pays, now divides the summit.

key_facts.fact: Roads around the venue were closed so that about 40 leaders could address the UN climate summit in Antalya on Wednesday 11 November; many ordinary delegates worked from hotels.

Antonio Guterres, giving his final COP speech as UN Secretary-General, proposed a 'climate justice compact' and said: 'We cannot demand that countries transform their economies while denying them the means to do so.'
Guterres said the case for fossil fuels 'is collapsing' and that three-quarters of people live in fossil fuel importing countries.
The '35 by 35' electrification pledge aims to raise electricity's share of global final energy consumption from 23% to 35% by 2035. It does not specify how the electricity is generated.

Public backers of the pledge so far: Australia, Ethiopia, Germany, Norway, Finland, Pakistan, Zimbabwe, Eswatini, Togo, Liechtenstein, Palau, Seychelles and the Solomon Islands. The full list is expected next week.

Palau said electrification 'must not become a substitute or a distraction' from transitioning away from fossil fuels. The Marshall Islands called the target 'insufficient' without a link to renewables and has not signed up. The EU and UK welcomed the focus but have not signed up.
Australia's climate minister Chris Bowen said an electric vehicle cuts emissions by 60% on a coal grid and 90% on solar.
Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said 'momentum without finance cannot be sustained'.
Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine said new fossil fuel discoveries are 'not something to celebrate, but to fear'.

Ethiopia, which hosts COP32 in Addis Ababa, gets more than 90% of its electricity from hydropower and has banned imports of internal combustion engine vehicles. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said every finance pledge should answer: 'How much? By when? On what terms?'
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said: 'The most vulnerable countries need capital. We must ensure they get it.'

Brazil's President Lula said science and multilateralism are 'under attack' and called for $1.3 trillion a year in climate finance by 2035; his speech was read by Joao Paulo Capobianco because of a raspy throat.

Finland published a plan to move electricity and district heating fully to low-carbon sources 'by the 2030s'; France, Germany and the Netherlands have also published domestic plans to phase out fossil fuels.
Pledges to Brazil's Tropical Forest Forever Facility total around $7.9bn, short of the $10bn startup target; Norway pledged $3bn, conditional on $10bn being mobilised by year-end.
Turkey plans new oil production and is expanding coal mining, as is Australia; President Erdogan did not address Turkey's own fossil fuel plans in his speech.
Guterres said fossil fuels 'must go the way of the dinosaurs, but that won't happen on its own', and said this was his final COP before he steps down in December.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader scheduled to address the summit. French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Italian PM Giorgia Meloni did not attend; Canada, Japan and India were expected to skip.
China's Xi Jinping was represented by Vice President Han Zheng. US President Donald Trump is not attending; he pulled the US out of the Paris Agreement.
Erdogan announced earlier in the week that Turkey had discovered new oil fields, which he called 'good news'; on Wednesday he called for a 'fair' energy transition.
Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman warned that 'the quest for carbon neutrality without guaranteeing energy security can undermine our efforts'.
The EU stressed that electrification must be 'clean'. The talks run until 20 November 2026. In 2023, nations first agreed to transition away from fossil fuels, but progress has been slow.
The pledge would expand electricity use through electrifying transport, buildings and industry. COP31 President Murat Kurum said the 'energy crisis has shocked us out of our complacency'.

A Climate Action Tracker analysis finds current policies would only bring electricity to 28% of final energy by the 2035 deadline. The International Energy Agency (IEA) says the 35% goal is within reach given strong political backing, and will lead a mechanism to track it.
The COP has over 68,500 registered participants; the venue is about 25 km from Antalya's centre.
The Australia-led Global Rooftop Solar Declaration aims to double solar-powered households to 300 million by 2030.
Kurum said: 'The age of electricity is taking shape.' More than 180 major companies, including Volvo, Uber, IKEA and Siemens, back faster electrification.

Electrification would expand electricity use for transport, building heating and industrial processes that now depend heavily on oil, gas and other fossil fuels; Kurum said the global energy crisis exposed the vulnerability of countries that rely on imported fossil fuels.

stories.headline: Fossil Fuel CO2 Emissions Are Set to Fall 0.4% in 2026, but Total CO2 Still Rises
stories.what_happened: The Global Carbon Budget, published on 10 November by more than 140 scientists, projects that carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will fall 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2 billion tonnes. Oil emissions fall 1.9% after the energy shock from the Iran conflict, and solar, wind and electric vehicles are growing. But with land-use change included, total CO2 rises to 43.3 billion tonnes, and India's emissions are projected to rise 4.4%.
stories.why_it_matters: A fall caused partly by an oil shock is not the same as a lasting turn; scientists say only structural change, such as more renewables and electric vehicles, would make emissions peak for good.

key_facts.fact: The 21st annual Global Carbon Budget report was published on 10 November 2026 as a pre-print in the journal Earth System Science Data; a peer-reviewed version will follow.
Fossil CO2 emissions are projected to fall 0.4% in 2026, to 38.2 billion tonnes.
Including land-use change, total CO2 emissions rise to 43.3 billion tonnes, up from 42.8 billion tonnes in 2025.
Oil emissions fall 1.9%, natural gas emissions fall 0.3% and coal emissions rise 0.6%. International aviation and shipping each fall 1%.
Land-use change emissions are projected to rise slightly to 5.1 billion tonnes, driven by peat fires and forest degradation in Southeast Asia during the onset of El Nino.
China's emissions are projected to fall 0.9%; China produces 32% of global fossil emissions and accounts for half of the emissions avoided through renewables and electric vehicles.
US emissions are projected to fall 1.3%, mainly from lower coal use after a spike in 2025. EU emissions fall 1.5% and Japan's fall 1%.
India's emissions are projected to rise 4.4%, above its 3.5% average annual growth over the past decade.
The remaining carbon budget for limiting warming to 1.5C is 150 billion tonnes, less than four years at the current rate.
Atmospheric CO2 reaches 427.7 parts per million in 2026, 54% above pre-industrial levels.
The decline in oil is likely a short-term response to an energy shock from the Iran conflict. Solar, wind and electric vehicles meet about two-thirds of rising energy demand.
The report was produced by more than 140 scientists; the team includes the University of Exeter, the University of East Anglia (UEA), CICERO and more than 90 other institutions.
Lead author Prof. Pierre Friedlingstein of the University of Exeter said 'a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution'.

Prof. Corinne Le Quere of UEA said: 'A further acceleration could turn the tide on global emissions within a few years.' Glen Peters of CICERO said: 'A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak unless it is driven by structural change.'
Total CO2 emissions grew 0.3% per year over the past decade, compared with 1.7% per year in the decade before. 59 countries emitted less in 2025 than in 2019 while growing their economies.
Emissions avoided by solar and wind rose from 0.28 billion tonnes in 2010 to 4.1 billion tonnes in 2025. Novel carbon dioxide removal offsets less than 30 minutes of annual fossil emissions.
The land sink (carbon absorbed by land plants) recovered after weakening during the 2023-24 El Nino; a strong 2026 El Nino is expected to affect it in the coming year.

The Wire reports the global decline is attributed mainly to the Iran conflict, which has effectively blocked the Strait of Hormuz, and to expanding solar and wind power; the US fall follows a spike the previous year linked to high gas prices and cold weather.
The study was released at COP31 in Antalya by the Global Carbon Project and led by the University of Exeter.

The fall would follow a record high in 2025 and would be the first annual decline since 2020, RTE reports. Le Quere said the drop is partly caused by high oil prices, which she called 'not a way to tackle climate change'.
Permanent deforestation emissions average about 3.8 billion tonnes of CO2 per year (2016-25); reforestation and afforestation offset about half of this.

stories.headline: Iran Denies Talks With the US and Says Hormuz Stays Shut Until Seven Conditions Are Met
stories.what_happened: Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei said on Tuesday 10 November that Tehran is still waiting for a US answer to its seven conditions for peace talks, and called reports of a meeting in Qatar 'a pure lie'. He said the Strait of Hormuz will stay closed until the conditions are met. President Trump said he saw 'positive momentum' and that new attacks on Iran were unnecessary.
stories.why_it_matters: The strait is a key route for the world's oil and gas; while it stays shut, fuel prices stay high around the world.

key_facts.fact: Mohsen Rezaei, Iran's security chief, said Tehran is awaiting a US response to its seven conditions for peace talks; he dismissed reports of negotiations and called claims of a meeting in Qatar 'a pure lie'.
Rezaei said Washington was talking up negotiations to ease economic pressure and lower oil prices; he called the initial US response 'insufficient and deceptive'.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Hormuz could reopen within two days if Iran's demands are met, and that the conflict will not be resolved through military means or intensified sanctions.

Iran has not published the full list of seven conditions; Rezaei and Araghchi say it includes lifting sanctions and the US naval blockade, and ending fighting on all fronts, especially Israel's attacks on Lebanon.
Iran closed the strait, and Rezaei said it will stay closed until the US meets the seven conditions.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said three oil tankers caught fire on Tuesday after hitting naval mines in an 'unauthorised route' in the eastern strait.
Maritime monitoring firms reported at least 37 attacks on ships in and near the strait in October, the highest monthly total since the war began.

Donald Trump said he saw 'positive momentum' toward ending the conflict and that new attacks on Iran were unnecessary; on Monday he met Qatar's Prime Minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, at the White House.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking in Paris, said Washington is 'open to diplomacy' and that further strikes weren't needed if the same objectives can be met through economic means.
Qatar is described as a key mediator. The war is in its ninth month and has disrupted oil and gas supplies, pushing prices up globally.

stories.headline: De Silva and Mendis Centuries Take Sri Lanka to 404-4 in the Rawalpindi Test
stories.what_happened: On day three of the first Test in Rawalpindi, Sri Lanka reached 404 for 4, 30 runs behind Pakistan's 434 for 9 declared. Dhananjaya de Silva was unbeaten on 167 and Kusal Mendis had made 117.
stories.why_it_matters: A long partnership turned the match around for Sri Lanka.

key_facts.fact: Sri Lanka were 404-4 after 102 overs against Pakistan's 434-9 declared in the first Test, with Dhananjaya de Silva on 167 and Kusal Mendis on 117.

Bad light stopped play with Sri Lanka at 404 for 4, just 30 runs behind Pakistan's 434 for 9 declared; de Silva and Mendis had added 249 runs without being separated, and the Rawalpindi Test was heading for a draw.

stories.headline: US Prices Rose 0.4% in October, More Than Expected, Raising the Odds of a Fed Rate Rise
stories.what_happened: The US Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in October from September, above the 0.3% economists expected, in a report released on Tuesday 10 November. Food rose 0.5%, energy 0.7% and housing 0.3%. Traders now see a strong chance that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December, and stocks fell.
stories.why_it_matters: When prices rise faster than expected, the central bank may raise interest rates, which makes mortgages and other loans cost more for families.

key_facts.fact: US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October from September, above the 0.3% economists expected but below September's 0.6% gain; the report was released on Tuesday morning.
Year-over-year figures were not published: the Bureau of Labor Statistics could not release full October 2025 data because of last year's government shutdown.
Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% from September, above the 0.2% expected and matching September's pace.
Energy prices rose 0.7%, down from 5.2% in September; housing rose 0.3%, a major contributor; food rose 0.5%.
Traders put an 84% chance on a quarter-point (25 basis point) rate rise at the Fed's December meeting; bets on a half-point rise went from 0% to 15%.
Fed Governor Chris Waller, speaking in London before the report, said: 'Inflation is too high.' He said a half-point rise should be considered in December if October inflation came in hot.
Waller said: 'Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.'
The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.93%; gold fell more than 2%.
The S&P 500 fell 0.4% to 7,520.93, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.3% and the Nasdaq composite fell 0.7% on Tuesday.
The report showed higher prices for groceries, electricity and other costs of living; inflation was higher last month than economists expected.
Waller had said that if the underlying measure of inflation rose 0.3%, the Fed should consider a half-point rise rather than the usual quarter-point; the measure rose exactly 0.3%.
Homebuilders' shares fell: Lennar lost 5.4% and D.R. Horton 3.8%, as higher interest rates make mortgages dearer.
Brent crude oil fell 1.2% to $91.49 a barrel; it was above $112 at the start of the month. President Trump said late Monday that the war in Iran 'militarily is effectively over'.
The 10-year Treasury yield had topped 5.30% in early October before falling.

stories.headline: House Sends Hegseth Impeachment Articles to a Committee, Halting the Effort
stories.what_happened: The US House of Representatives voted 211-204 on Tuesday 10 November to refer eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the House Judiciary Committee, a procedural step that effectively halted the effort. Republican Thomas Massie of Kentucky had introduced the articles. On Wednesday, at a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery, President Trump praised Hegseth.
stories.why_it_matters: The vote shows how Congress can check, or decline to check, a member of the president's Cabinet, and how a procedural motion can settle a question without a direct vote on it.

key_facts.fact: The House voted 211-204 on Tuesday to refer eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the House Judiciary Committee; this procedural motion effectively halted the effort.
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced the articles.
Eleven Democrats were recorded as not voting; eight more votes against the motion would have defeated it.
The vote was on a motion to refer, not a direct vote on impeachment itself.

The articles allege violating congressional war powers by conducting military operations against Iran without authorization, continuing the Iran conflict despite congressional opposition, and disregarding protections for civilians.

They also allege authorizing unlawful strikes against suspected drug-trafficking vessels, participating in the capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro, and retaliating against Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona over his public statements about military orders.

The committee could consider the allegations and recommend further action, but it is not required to; the referral makes further proceedings unlikely before the current Republican-controlled Congress ends.
Democrats are set to take control of the House in January, which could open the door to a renewed impeachment push.

At the annual Veterans Day tribute at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday, Trump praised Hegseth: 'He's done a fantastic job, and he loves you and he protects you.' Trump said he 'had a feeling that was going to happen'.

President Trump, Vice President JD Vance and First Lady Melania Trump took part in the 2026 National Veterans Day wreath-laying ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday 11 November; Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth attended.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries would not say whether Democrats will try to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth once they have the majority.

stories.headline: India's Cabinet Approves a Rs 62,370 Crore Fertiliser Subsidy for the Winter Crop Season, Up 64%
stories.what_happened: India's Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Wednesday 11 November approved subsidy rates for phosphatic and potassic fertilisers for the Rabi (winter) 2026-27 season. The estimated cost is Rs 62,370.02 crore, about 64% more than last Rabi season, because international prices of fertilisers and their raw materials have risen. It was one of five proposals approved, worth Rs 77,101 crore together.
stories.why_it_matters: India imports much of its fertiliser, so when world prices jump the government must choose between higher costs for farmers and a bigger bill for taxpayers; this time it chose to pay.

key_facts.fact: The Union Cabinet, chaired by PM Narendra Modi, approved Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) rates for phosphatic and potassic (P&K) fertilisers for the Rabi 2026-27 season on Wednesday 11 November 2026.
The tentative subsidy requirement is Rs 62,370.02 crore, about 64% higher than the previous year: roughly Rs 24,417.73 crore more than the Rs 37,952.29 crore for the 2025-26 Rabi season.
The approved rates apply from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027.

The subsidy covers P&K fertilisers including di-ammonium phosphate (DAP) and NPKS grades; the government provides 28 grades of P&K fertilisers at subsidised prices through manufacturers and importers.
The NBS scheme has been in place since 1 April 2010; subsidies go to fertiliser companies at approved rates so that fertilisers reach farmers at affordable prices.
The Cabinet cited 'rationalisation' of subsidies in view of recent trends in international prices of fertilisers and inputs: urea, DAP, muriate of potash (MOP) and sulphur.
Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, at the Cabinet briefing, said domestic manufacturing will increase and farmers will not face any additional burden.
Under the scheme the subsidy is based on each fertiliser's nutrient content, not a uniform per-product subsidy; it covers four nutrients: nitrogen (N), phosphate (P), potash (K) and sulphur (S).

India depends heavily on imports for its phosphatic and potassic fertilisers and their raw materials, so global price swings in DAP, MOP, phosphoric acid, ammonia and sulphur significantly affect domestic subsidy needs.
Rabi is the six-month winter season, during which crops such as wheat, mustard and pulses need adequate nutrients.
S Sankarasubramanian, chairman of the Fertiliser Association of India (FAI), called the decision timely and positive.
The increase is about 64.3% over the previous Rabi season.
On 11 November 2026 the Cabinet approved five proposals with a combined outlay of Rs 77,101 crore. Urea is outside the NBS framework.
The Cabinet approved an 8.45 km extension of the Noida Metro Aqua Line, from Noida Sector 51 to Greater Noida Sector 4, with five elevated stations, costing Rs 2,390 crore.
The Cabinet approved Rs 3,230 crore for the Yuge Yugeen Bharat National Museum in New Delhi, to be made by reusing the historic North Block and South Block buildings.

The Stand-Up India scheme was extended for five years to 31 March 2031, with a Rs 4,111 crore credit guarantee corpus, expected to support 2.5 lakh more women, Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe entrepreneurs.
The Credit Guarantee Fund for Micro Units was extended to 31 March 2031 with a corpus of Rs 5,000 crore; it covers lenders against default on loans under the Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana.

stories.geography: India; New Delhi, where the Union Cabinet meets; Noida and Greater Noida in Uttar Pradesh

Food rose 0.5%, energy 0.7% and housing 0.3%. Traders now see a strong chance that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December, and stocks fell.
stories.why_it_matters: When prices rise faster than expected, the central bank may raise interest rates, which makes mortgages and other loans cost more for families.

key_facts.fact: US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October from September, above the 0.3% economists expected but below September's 0.6% gain; the report was released on Tuesday morning.
Year-over-year figures were not published: the Bureau of Labor Statistics could not release full October 2025 data because of last year's government shutdown.
Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% from September, above the 0.2% expected and matching September's pace.
Energy prices rose 0.7%, down from 5.2% in September; housing rose 0.3%, a major contributor; food rose 0.5%.
Traders put an 84% chance on a quarter-point (25 basis point) rate rise at the Fed's December meeting; bets on a half-point rise went from 0% to 15%.
Fed Governor Chris Waller, speaking in London before the report, said: 'Inflation is too high.' He said a half-point rise should be considered in December if October inflation came in hot.
Waller said: 'Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.'
The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.93%; gold fell more than 2%.
The S&P 500 fell 0.4% to 7,520.93, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.3% and the Nasdaq composite fell 0.7% on Tuesday.
The report showed higher prices for groceries, electricity and other costs of living; inflation was higher last month than economists expected.
Waller had said that if the underlying measure of inflation rose 0.3%, the Fed should consider a half-point rise rather than the usual quarter-point; the measure rose exactly 0.3%.
Homebuilders' shares fell: Lennar lost 5.4% and D.R. Horton 3.8%, as higher interest rates make mortgages dearer.
Brent crude oil fell 1.2% to $91.49 a barrel; it was above $112 at the start of the month. President Trump said late Monday that the war in Iran 'militarily is effectively over'.
The 10-year Treasury yield had topped 5.30% in early October before falling.

stories.headline: India's Cabinet Approves a Rs 62,370 Crore Fertiliser Subsidy for the Winter Crop Season, Up 64%
stories.what_happened: India's Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Wednesday 11 November approved subsidy rates for phosphatic and potassic fertilisers for the Rabi (winter) 2026-27 season. The estimated cost is Rs 62,370.02 crore, about 64% more than last Rabi season, because international prices of fertilisers and their raw materials have risen. It was one of five proposals approved, worth Rs 77,101 crore together.
stories.why_it_matters: India imports much of its fertiliser, so when world prices jump the government must choose between higher costs for farmers and a bigger bill for taxpayers; this time it chose to pay.

key_facts.fact: The Union Cabinet, chaired by PM Narendra Modi, approved Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) rates for phosphatic and potassic (P&K) fertilisers for the Rabi 2026-27 season on Wednesday 11 November 2026.
The tentative subsidy requirement is Rs 62,370.02 crore, about 64% higher than the previous year: roughly Rs 24,417.73 crore more than the Rs 37,952.29 crore for the 2025-26 Rabi season.
The approved rates apply from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027.

The subsidy covers P&K fertilisers including di-ammonium phosphate (DAP) and NPKS grades; the government provides 28 grades of P&K fertilisers at subsidised prices through manufacturers and importers.
The NBS scheme has been in place since 1 April 2010; subsidies go to fertiliser companies at approved rates so that fertilisers reach farmers at affordable prices.
The Cabinet cited 'rationalisation' of subsidies in view of recent trends in international prices of fertilisers and inputs: urea, DAP, muriate of potash (MOP) and sulphur.
Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, at the Cabinet briefing, said domestic manufacturing will increase and farmers will not face any additional burden.
Under the scheme the subsidy is based on each fertiliser's nutrient content, not a uniform per-product subsidy; it covers four nutrients: nitrogen (N), phosphate (P), potash (K) and sulphur (S).

India depends heavily on imports for its phosphatic and potassic fertilisers and their raw materials, so global price swings in DAP, MOP, phosphoric acid, ammonia and sulphur significantly affect domestic subsidy needs.
Rabi is the six-month winter season, during which crops such as wheat, mustard and pulses need adequate nutrients.
S Sankarasubramanian, chairman of the Fertiliser Association of India (FAI), called the decision timely and positive.
The increase is about 64.3% over the previous Rabi season.
On 11 November 2026 the Cabinet approved five proposals with a combined outlay of Rs 77,101 crore. Urea is outside the NBS framework.
The Cabinet approved an 8.45 km extension of the Noida Metro Aqua Line, from Noida Sector 51 to Greater Noida Sector 4, with five elevated stations, costing Rs 2,390 crore.
The Cabinet approved Rs 3,230 crore for the Yuge Yugeen Bharat National Museum in New Delhi, to be made by reusing the historic North Block and South Block buildings.

The Stand-Up India scheme was extended for five years to 31 March 2031, with a Rs 4,111 crore credit guarantee corpus, expected to support 2.5 lakh more women, Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe entrepreneurs.
The Credit Guarantee Fund for Micro Units was extended to 31 March 2031 with a corpus of Rs 5,000 crore; it covers lenders against default on loans under the Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana.

stories.headline: Four EU Countries Defy Germany's Merz Over Tying the Next EU Budget to Ukraine Aid
stories.what_happened: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told European Council President Antonio Costa in a letter that fresh aid for Ukraine is an 'essential prerequisite' for approving the EU's next long-term budget. Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria objected; Slovakia's Robert Fico called it a 'textbook case of blackmail'. Costa replied by promising a wide discussion on Ukraine at an informal leaders' meeting in Dublin on 13 November, with a special summit in Brussels on 26-27 November.
stories.why_it_matters: Both the EU budget and Ukraine aid need every member country to agree, so a single government can block either, and Ukraine faces a 70 billion euro gap next year.

key_facts.fact: In a letter to European Council President Antonio Costa, Merz said fresh Ukraine aid is an 'essential prerequisite' for approving the next EU budget; he repeated the position in Berlin on 10 November.
Both the budget and Ukraine aid require unanimity among EU countries.

Kyiv faces a 70 billion euro shortfall next year; Brussels has promised to cover about two-thirds, roughly 45 billion euros, through an instrument not yet defined. New joint debt has emerged as the frontrunner option.
The proposed next long-term budget already earmarks 100 billion euros for Ukraine, but those funds are not available until 2028.
The new funding would come on top of an existing 90 billion euro support loan, from which Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Hungary received exemptions.
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico called Merz's move a 'textbook case of blackmail' and threatened to use his veto: 'We have an equal say in this matter.'
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis said Merz 'probably doesn't realise' the budget already earmarks 100 billion euros for Ukraine.

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar opposes linking the issues but said 'I do not consider this to be blackmail'; he said Hungary cannot take on fresh EU-level debt because of its deficit, and added: 'We will find a solution for the EU budget.'
Bulgaria's Rumen Radev cited high deficits as grounds for exemption from future Ukraine credit lines and said Bulgaria is 'in no way blocking' Council decisions.

The four belong to the 'Friends of Cohesion', a group of 17 countries seeking to protect cohesion and agricultural funds; they are opposed by the 'frugals', including Germany, who want across-the-board cuts. Germany is one of Ukraine's largest donors.
Costa replied to Merz by promising a wide-ranging discussion on Ukraine, including its funding needs for 2027, at the informal EU leaders' meeting in Dublin on 13 November 2026.

A special EU summit in Brussels on 26-27 November 2026 will address Ukraine's 2027 financial needs and the EU's next multiannual financial framework, the budget for 2028-2034; the European Commission is expected to submit a proposal on Ukraine's funding before then.
The 90 billion euro loan for Ukraine covers 2026-2027. Italian PM Giorgia Meloni had asked Costa who would represent the EU in peace negotiations on Ukraine.

stories.headline: Fossil Fuel CO2 Emissions Are Set to Fall 0.4% in 2026, but Total CO2 Still Rises
stories.what_happened: The Global Carbon Budget, published on 10 November by more than 140 scientists, projects that carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will fall 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2 billion tonnes. Oil emissions fall 1.9% after the energy shock from the Iran conflict, and solar, wind and electric vehicles are growing. But with land-use change included, total CO2 rises to 43.3 billion tonnes, and India's emissions are projected to rise 4.4%.
stories.why_it_matters: A fall caused partly by an oil shock is not the same as a lasting turn; scientists say only structural change, such as more renewables and electric vehicles, would make emissions peak for good.

key_facts.fact: The 21st annual Global Carbon Budget report was published on 10 November 2026 as a pre-print in the journal Earth System Science Data; a peer-reviewed version will follow.
Fossil CO2 emissions are projected to fall 0.4% in 2026, to 38.2 billion tonnes.
Including land-use change, total CO2 emissions rise to 43.3 billion tonnes, up from 42.8 billion tonnes in 2025.
Oil emissions fall 1.9%, natural gas emissions fall 0.3% and coal emissions rise 0.6%. International aviation and shipping each fall 1%.
Land-use change emissions are projected to rise slightly to 5.1 billion tonnes, driven by peat fires and forest degradation in Southeast Asia during the onset of El Nino.
China's emissions are projected to fall 0.9%; China produces 32% of global fossil emissions and accounts for half of the emissions avoided through renewables and electric vehicles.
US emissions are projected to fall 1.3%, mainly from lower coal use after a spike in 2025. EU emissions fall 1.5% and Japan's fall 1%.
India's emissions are projected to rise 4.4%, above its 3.5% average annual growth over the past decade.
The remaining carbon budget for limiting warming to 1.5C is 150 billion tonnes, less than four years at the current rate.
Atmospheric CO2 reaches 427.7 parts per million in 2026, 54% above pre-industrial levels.
The decline in oil is likely a short-term response to an energy shock from the Iran conflict. Solar, wind and electric vehicles meet about two-thirds of rising energy demand.
The report was produced by more than 140 scientists; the team includes the University of Exeter, the University of East Anglia (UEA), CICERO and more than 90 other institutions.
Lead author Prof. Pierre Friedlingstein of the University of Exeter said 'a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution'.

Prof. Corinne Le Quere of UEA said: 'A further acceleration could turn the tide on global emissions within a few years.' Glen Peters of CICERO said: 'A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak unless it is driven by structural change.'
Total CO2 emissions grew 0.3% per year over the past decade, compared with 1.7% per year in the decade before. 59 countries emitted less in 2025 than in 2019 while growing their economies.
Emissions avoided by solar and wind rose from 0.28 billion tonnes in 2010 to 4.1 billion tonnes in 2025. Novel carbon dioxide removal offsets less than 30 minutes of annual fossil emissions.
The land sink (carbon absorbed by land plants) recovered after weakening during the 2023-24 El Nino; a strong 2026 El Nino is expected to affect it in the coming year.

The Wire reports the global decline is attributed mainly to the Iran conflict, which has effectively blocked the Strait of Hormuz, and to expanding solar and wind power; the US fall follows a spike the previous year linked to high gas prices and cold weather.
The study was released at COP31 in Antalya by the Global Carbon Project and led by the University of Exeter.

The fall would follow a record high in 2025 and would be the first annual decline since 2020, RTE reports. Le Quere said the drop is partly caused by high oil prices, which she called 'not a way to tackle climate change'.
Permanent deforestation emissions average about 3.8 billion tonnes of CO2 per year (2016-25); reforestation and afforestation offset about half of this.

stories.headline: A 'Digital Twin' of the Webb Telescope Reveals a Planet Hidden in a Star's Glare
stories.what_happened: Researchers have found a previously hidden exoplanet in existing James Webb Space Telescope images by using a new technique called FLIP. They built a detailed computer model, a 'digital twin', of the telescope's camera, used it to work out exactly how a star's light appears in an image, and subtracted that light to reveal fainter objects nearby. The study was published in Nature on 4 November.
stories.why_it_matters: Planets are vastly fainter than their stars; a method that sees two to fifteen times fainter objects could help future telescopes photograph Earth-like worlds.

key_facts.fact: A previously hidden exoplanet was found in existing James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) data.
The technique gave 2 to 15 times greater detection sensitivity than conventional methods in tests with known planets.
The technique is called FLIP, for Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets.

The team built a 'digital twin', a physical model of JWST's Near Infrared Camera (NIRCam), and used computation to examine millions of possible imperfections and unknown factors that affect the observations.
This produces a highly precise model of how the star appears in the image; the modeled starlight is subtracted from the original observations, revealing dimmer objects nearby.
Machine learning optimization tools adjust millions of variables until the simulation matches the real data.
The team's first approach, training machine learning models to predict starlight patterns, failed, so they switched to physics-based modeling.

Lead author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez is a graduate student at Northwestern University in the lab of Jason Wang; he began the project as an undergraduate at the Autonomous University of Yucatan in Mexico.
Co-authors include Katherine Bouman and Dimitri Mawet of Caltech and researchers at MIT and the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore.
The paper, 'Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit', was published online in Nature on 4 November 2026.

JWST is optically stable to the nanometer level, which the researchers say still limits detection. Jason Wang said: 'We've now gone beyond the telescope stability limit for the first time with this new technique.'
An Earth-like planet orbiting a Sun-like star can be about 10 billion times fainter than its star.

NASA's proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory aims to directly image Earth-like planets in the habitable zones of Sun-like stars; the team plans to test FLIP with NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and ground-based telescopes.
Katie Bouman said even the tiniest imperfections in a telescope can make it difficult to separate the faint light of a planet from its star.

stories.headline: UK Weighs Cutting Its Electric Car Sales Targets as Burnham Says No Decision Has Been Made
stories.what_happened: Reports say the UK government is poised to cut its 2030 target for electric car sales from 80% of new cars to roughly 60%. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on 11 November that the reports are speculation and no decision has been made. Electric cars made up 26.6% of new car registrations in January to October, below this year's 33% headline target.
stories.why_it_matters: The rule decides how quickly Britain's new cars switch from petrol and diesel to electric; carmakers say it runs ahead of what buyers want, while climate groups say weakening it would slow emissions cuts.

key_facts.fact: Prime Minister Andy Burnham denied the government will announce an overhaul of the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) Mandate this week: 'they're reports, they're speculation and no decision has been made at this point'.
The Guardian reported that Louise Haigh is expected to agree this week to cut the EV sales target by about a quarter.
The motor industry and dealers have lobbied for significant cuts to the targets, arguing the mandate is distorting the market.
Battery electric cars made up 26.6% of UK new car registrations in January-October 2026, with 503,805 registered; in October alone the share was 32.0%. The 2026 headline car target is 33%.
Electric vans had an 11% market share in January-October, against a 24% target.
Burnham is due to attend the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, his first as Prime Minister.
The ZEV mandate became law on 3 January 2024 under the Conservatives; it sets annual EV sales targets for manufacturers, rising towards 2030.
Each manufacturer must meet its own target or use regulatory flexibilities; otherwise it faces significant financial penalties.
The original car target was 22% in 2024, rising to 80% by 2030; the government says it is committed to 100% zero-emission new car and van sales by 2035.
Under the reported change, the 2030 car target would be cut by about a quarter, to roughly 60%; Louise Haigh, First Secretary of State, is reportedly poised to finalise the changes.
A government spokesperson said 'no decisions have been taken'. Labour's consultation explored four alternative policy paths.
Manufacturers met their targets in 2024 and 2025 using flexibilities, and are expected to do so again in 2026.
The SMMT, the car industry body, says the mandate runs ahead of natural demand, forcing companies to subsidise the market.

Ben Plowden of the Campaign for Better Transport said weakening the mandate would be a 'major setback' for cutting transport emissions; Dominic Phinn of Climate Group said weakening it in the week of COP31 'beggars belief'.

Climate Home News reports Burnham will stay out of the decision because his wife advises the board of an EV-charging network; a meeting on the issue was set for Wednesday, presided over by Louise Haigh.

stories.headline: The UK Falls Silent for Two Minutes on Armistice Day
stories.what_happened: At 11:00 on Wednesday 11 November the UK observed a two-minute silence for Armistice Day across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting laid a wreath at the Cenotaph in London.
stories.why_it_matters: The silence marks the moment fighting stopped in World War One in 1918, and remembers those who died in wars since.

key_facts.fact: The UK observed a two-minute silence at 11:00 on 11 November across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
The Armistice was an agreement to end fighting in World War One, as a prelude to peace negotiations; it began at 11:00 on 11 November 1918.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting laid a wreath at the Cenotaph in London; the 110th anniversary of the Battle of the Somme was marked at the ceremony.
At the start of Prime Minister's Questions, Andy Burnham paid tribute to 'all those who made the ultimate sacrifice for our country'.
In Edinburgh the one o'clock gun at Edinburgh Castle fired at 11:00 to start the silence; in Conwy, north Wales, schoolchildren read out the names of the fallen.
In Paris, French President Emmanuel Macron laid a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

stories.headline: Abu Dhabi Talks End With a Large Prisoner Exchange Agreed but No Ceasefire
stories.what_happened: Two days of US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi ended on Wednesday 11 November with an agreement in principle on a large exchange of prisoners of war. There was no breakthrough on a ceasefire or on territory. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are due to meet Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday and then Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Dublin.
stories.why_it_matters: The exchange would bring many captured soldiers home, but the questions that decide whether the war ends, territory and security, remain unsettled, and Europe is still outside the main room.

key_facts.fact: Two days of US-mediated Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, ended on Wednesday 11 November 2026 with an agreement in principle on a major prisoner exchange.
The exchange was the only tangible result; there was no breakthrough on a ceasefire or on territorial disputes.
US envoy Jared Kushner announced the deal on Wednesday and said the final prisoner numbers would be set on Thursday.
Kushner called it 'the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners' and 'one of the positives'.
Ukraine's chief negotiator Rustem Umerov and Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky both confirmed the exchange; neither gave details on timing or scale.
On Tuesday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said negotiators had discussed exchanging 1,000 prisoners from each side, possibly rising to 1,500 each.
These were the first direct Kyiv-Moscow negotiations in nine months; an earlier round in Geneva in February 2026 produced no breakthrough.
In May 2025, talks in Istanbul also produced an agreement to exchange 1,000 prisoners each, without a ceasefire.
Kushner said of a Putin-Zelenskyy meeting that more work is needed: 'we are pushing a boulder uphill'. He said 'there is not great trust or love between the leaders'.
Kushner said the US speaks daily with both Zelenskyy's team and Putin's team.
Kushner and Steve Witkoff were to travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet Putin, then go to Dublin for talks with Zelenskyy.

Ukrainian negotiator Davyd Arakhamia described the talks as among the most difficult, said Russian representatives had strict instructions, and called for another round 'as soon as possible', hoping for a solution before the new year.
Zelenskyy, on a state visit to Copenhagen, was briefed by video call; he said 'ending this war and providing security guarantees' must come first.
Russia demands that Ukraine withdraw from the part of the Donbas region still under Kyiv's control; Zelenskyy says territorial decisions must be made at the leaders' level.
Moscow rejects an immediate ceasefire and wants broader security arrangements first.
European representatives were in Abu Dhabi for separate consultations with Ukrainian and US officials; they did not take part in the trilateral talks.
Medinsky said Russia had not held talks with Europeans: 'We don't really understand in what capacity they are here.' He said Moscow had received no concrete European peace proposals.
Washington indicated that European countries should eventually join the negotiations, particularly on future security arrangements.
The talks focused mainly on humanitarian issues: prisoner exchanges, returning Ukrainian civilians held in captivity, and children taken from Ukraine. Security guarantees were also discussed.
Medinsky said mutual understanding was reached on some issues and more talks will be held.
Zelenskyy, who was in Copenhagen and did not attend, called the second day 'constructive and quite substantive'.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the meeting 'very productive' but said a breakthrough to end the war will take time.
Representatives from European governments, the EU and NATO were in Abu Dhabi and consulted with Ukraine's delegation. Zelenskyy said European security cannot be considered 'without Europe'.
Ukraine is reeling from aerial attacks on its power grid; little territory has changed hands on the front line this year; the war has lasted nearly five years.

Overnight, Russia struck Zaporizhzhia and Kharkiv, wounding seven civilians. Russia's Defence Ministry said it downed 627 Ukrainian drones overnight; drones started a fire at the Ust-Luga port, a major oil export facility.
The final session on Wednesday ran just under two hours. Medinsky, an adviser to President Putin, said details of the exchange would be announced 'shortly'.
Medinsky said security arrangements for Ukraine and Europe were a central focus: 'In some places we reached an understanding, in other places we did not.'

Medinsky repeated Moscow's claim to parts of Ukraine: 'every inch of our land will be returned to Russia. One way or another.' Ukraine rejects giving up any territory it currently controls as a condition for peace.
Russia's broader demands include territorial concessions, demilitarisation and major political changes in Kyiv.

US officials told the Financial Times they want to resolve the war and continental security arrangements together and that European officials should have a seat at the table; Moscow has so far rejected a European role.
Zelenskyy landed in Ireland on Wednesday 11 November and met Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheal Martin at Government Buildings in Dublin.
In Dublin, Zelenskyy said between 1,000 and 1,200 prisoners of war may be exchanged.
The European Political Community (EPC) summit is in Dublin on Thursday 12 November at the Convention Centre Dublin; Zelenskyy is due to speak. Ireland holds the EU Council presidency for six months.
Kushner said the Dublin meeting would be a 'debrief' and that the US sees 'some openings and some opportunities'.
On the Donbas region, Zelenskyy said Ukraine could not discuss abandoning it. The Taoiseach said Ukrainians deserve a 'just and lasting peace' and that Ukraine's future 'is in the European Union'.

Moscow also wants a ban on Ukrainian NATO membership and limits on Ukraine's military. Ukraine proposes an unconditional ceasefire as the first step toward broader talks; the Kremlin has repeatedly dismissed this.
Donbas is a partially occupied, strategically important region in eastern Ukraine. Zelensky will attend an informal meeting of EU leaders on 13 November.
